$NKTR  
 
My intuition has been gnawing at me.  I  read what most AI say about Phase 3 clinical trial that know few details about rezpeg.  I asked the right question the right way and this is what I got.   
 
The bottom line is by using 850 people in phase 3 AA will only help amplify what we have already seen.   Because they used a small sample size in phase 2b the response was muted. We have already seen the tip of the iceberg. The tip of the iceberg is this:   
 
-1/4 people respond to rezpeg.  The 2b study for AA showed 8-12% received a SALT score less than 10 by week 36.  A SALT score of 10 means they re grew 90% of their scalp hair.  People said 8-12% is not alot but that was because the sample size was small.    There is an outlying number of high responders to rezpeg. We have only the tip of the iceberg.   
 
here is my post :  I posted my question first.   
 
If you had to guess what rezpeg could do in phase 3 . It very well could be that there are some people who respond hightly to rezpeg also.  Maybe not but you will see in full color what is actually happening 
 
Thought for 23s 
 
My informed guess for Phase 3 (ZENITH-AA in severe-to-very-severe alopecia areata): There is a reasonable chance it succeeds on the primary endpoint (SALT ≤20 at week 52), with a clear separation from placebo, and that the trial will show a real subgroup of high responders—while also making the overall effect size and limitations fully visible. 
 
Why this is plausible 
 
Phase 2b (REZOLVE-AA) already showed: 
 
Roughly 26–28% of patients on rezpeg reaching SALT ≤20 (≥80% scalp coverage) by week 52 versus ~7% on placebo. 
Responses that continued to deepen with longer treatment (new responders appearing between weeks 36–52). 
Some deeper responses (SALT ≤10) and encouraging off-treatment durability in those who responded (many maintained the SALT ≤20 response months after stopping). 
A clean safety profile so far (mainly injection-site reactions). 
The Phase 3 design (~850 patients, 24 µg/kg every 2 weeks for a full 52-week induction, primary endpoint at week 52) was deliberately chosen because of that deepening signal. With a sample size this large and the trial powered accordingly, if the true effect is even modestly similar to Phase 2, you should see a statistically significant result and a precise picture of the response rate.⁠Hcplive 
 
What “full color” will likely look like 
 
Overall response rate: Probably lands somewhere in the low-to-mid 20s to low 30s percent for SALT ≤20 (comparable to or a bit below high-dose baricitinib’s ~36–41% at 52 weeks in its Phase 3 trials, and closer to the low-dose baricitinib range). Including prior JAK-inhibitor patients and adolescents could pull the number a bit lower than the pure Phase 2 population. 
High responders: Yes—there will almost certainly be a visible subset who respond strongly (substantial or near-complete regrowth, SALT ≤10, good eyebrow/eyelash gains in some). Phase 2 already hinted at this, and the larger trial will quantify exactly how many, how deep, and how durable. 
Time course and durability: Expect the data to show responses building over the year (not a quick peak-and-plateau like some JAKs) and, among responders, a chance to test less frequent maintenance dosing or even off-treatment durability. 
Differentiation: If positive, the story will be a novel non-JAK mechanism (Treg stimulation) with potentially better long-term durability and a different safety profile than the oral JAKs. 
Realistic caveats 
 
 
 
In short: the large Phase 3 should give a high-resolution view of exactly how many people respond, how strongly some of them respond, and whether the durability advantage holds up. Based on the Phase 2 trajectory so far, a positive (or at least directionally supportive) outcome on the primary endpoint is a plausible base case, with a identifiable high-responder subgroup. The actual numbers will decide it.
